extracted.intended_audience: students, naturalists, and researchers in zoology/taxonomy studying Hydra and related Hydrozoa
extracted.subtask_description: Diagnostic and observational criteria for identifying, describing, and studying Hydra species (morphology, reproduction, life-history, and behaviour), with keys, measurements, and field/aquarium observation notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species identification key (H. viridis, H. vulgaris, H. oligactis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dichotomous key distinguishing three recognized species: I. Colour leaf-green; cells contain green (chlorophyll) corpuscles; A. tentacles comparatively stout, habitually shorter than the column; egg-shell without spines, ornamented with a reticulate pattern = viridis. II. Colour never leaf-green; no chlorophyll corpuscles present. A. Tentacles capable of great elongation but when at rest never much longer than the column (which is cylindrical when gastral cavity empty); largest nettle-cells almost as broad as long; egg-shell bearing long spines most of which are divided at tips = vulgaris. B. Tentacles, even at rest, much longer than the column, basal part of column constricted even when gastral cavity empty; largest nettle-cells considerably longer than broad; egg-shell smooth or bearing short, simple spines = oligactis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multiple characters together (colour/chlorophyll bodies, tentacle length relative to column, shape/relative proportions of largest nettle-cells, and egg‑shell ornamentation). Use the combination of characters rather than any single trait because seasonal or geographic phases may alter some features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus Hydra diagnostic description
rubrics_metrics.description: Freshwater polyps which produce eggs with hard chitinous shells; habitually anchored by the aboral disk but possess considerable powers of locomotion; extremely contractile and variable in form and size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this genus-level description to separate Hydra (fresh/brackish water, chitinous-shelled eggs, contractile column, movement ability) from other soft sessile coelenterates when identifying specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Hydridæ characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Small Eleutheroblastea in which the mouth is surrounded by hollow tentacles. Permanent colonies are not formed, but reproduction by budding commonly takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence of hollow tentacles around the mouth and solitary (non-colonial) habit with frequent budding to recognize family Hydridæ among hydrozoans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nettle-cell (nematocyst) morphology as diagnostic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Nettle-cells (capsules) are very variable in size but in H. vulgaris are invariably broad in proportion to their length and usually nearly spherical. Capsules with barbed threads bear a basal circle of stout prominent spines (usually 4) and many very small spines above; capsules with unbarbed threads are broadly oval with rounded ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and compare capsule breadth and length and examine thread/barb structure; provided measurements (example: winter largest capsules ~0.0189 mm breadth × 0.019 mm length; summer ~0.012 mm breadth) illustrate seasonal variability and can aid identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egg and reproductive organ morphology for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Eggs are spherical; egg-shell bears relatively long spines expanded and flattened and often divided at the tip (in H. vulgaris phase orientalis). Spermaries are mammillate in form and number from 4 to 24. Ovaries and spermaries are not found on the same individual in the Indian material described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egg-shell ornament (long divided spines vs smooth or short simple spines) is an important species character. Note that eggs without shells may occur (probably unfertilized). Record presence/number/shape of spermaries and ovaries as diagnostic; sexual characters may be seasonally expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budding: position, order, and timing as observational criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Buds confined to a narrow zone nearer the base than the apex; each quadrant of the column can produce a single bud in a definite zone; on observed individuals buds appear in a fixed quadrant order (north, east, south, west pattern) though production timing can vary; about three weeks elapse from first appearance to liberation; rarely more than two attached simultaneously in some observations and exceptional cases may have up to four.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing reproductive mode or staging specimens, record bud position (zone), quadrant sequence, number present, and time to liberation. Note whether attached buds themselves produce buds (attached buds apparently never bud in the described race).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal brood forms and their distinguishing traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Two broods in Calcutta: a cold‑weather brood (larger, stouter, more deeply coloured, buds more freely, larger nematocysts, usually 6 tentacles; known to become sexually mature) and a hot‑weather brood (smaller, slender, paler, produces buds sparingly, smaller nematocysts, usually 4–5 tentacles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish seasonal phases when identifying specimens: many morphological characters (size, colour, nematocyst size, tentacle count, sexual maturity) vary systematically with season; failure to account for seasonal phase can lead to misidentification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of reproduction and their morphological signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Main modes: budding (common), sexual reproduction (eggs and spermaries; eggs rare in Indian field conditions), and fission (rare: equal and unequal vertical fission observed). In equal vertical fission the circumoral area lengthens, extra tentacles appear, the mouth constricts in the middle and the animal divides into two equal halves; transverse fission not observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record reproduction mode carefully: budding zone and liberated buds versus signs of fission (constriction, paired halves) versus presence of gametes. Note environmental stimuli suspected to influence sexual organ development (starvation, low oxygen, high temperature, lack of light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral and locomotory observations as identification/contextual data
rubrics_metrics.description: Hydra can float free (mouth uppermost or aboral pole at surface) and can crawl rapidly by alternately attaching tentacles and basal disk; movement involves adhesive secretions from gland-cells and tentacle attachment; tentacles can extend greatly and attach by tips, sometimes producing pseudopodia-like projections under mechanical strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observing behavior (field or aquarium), note modes of locomotion (floating vs crawling), attachment method, tentacle extension patterns, and responses to light/heat, since these behaviours inform ecological interpretation and may differ among forms or conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding behaviour, diet, and digestion indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Tentacles capture prey (chiefly larvæ of midges and may-flies, also small copepod and phyllopod crustacea). Prey is paralysed by nematocysts, brought to mouth by tentacle contraction and mucus, digested partly in upper cavity with gland-cell secretions and partly by endoderm cells; insoluble parts ejected. Colour of the polyp appears largely due to digestion products; well-fed or egg‑producing individuals may be coloured, starved ones nearly colourless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prey types, tentacle extension patterns (extended morning feeding), and digestive residue/colour to assess feeding status and health. Colour changes can indicate recent feeding/digestion, starvation, or reproductive state (egg producers often dark green).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological measurements and variability to record
rubrics_metrics.description: Column length commonly about 15 mm but can extend to nearly 30 mm when fully stretched; tentacle count usually 4–6 (occasionally 8); nematocyst sizes vary seasonally (examples provided: winter largest capsules ~0.0189 mm breadth × 0.019 mm length; summer ~0.012 mm breadth). Abnormal individuals (e.g., missing tentacles) occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take standardized measurements (column length when extended, tentacle number, nematocyst dimensions) and record season/location to account for intraspecific variation. Note abnormalities separately as they may reflect injury or developmental anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egg development and embryology (developmental stages and envelope formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fertilization occurs at the base of the ectoderm with spermatozoon boring through; after emergence segmentation forms a hollow mass of large equal cells, smaller cells fill cavity, a mucus film secreted, then larger cells secrete a thick chitinous egg-shell and an inner delicate membrane; development may be delayed, repeated cell division forms an oval hollow embryo which escapes by disintegration of egg-shell and rupture of inner membrane; tentacles and mouth form subsequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When staging embryos or eggs, look for the mucus film, chitinous shell, inner membrane, and timing of cell divisions. Note that development can be delayed and that the egg-shell may retain debris which conceals it prior to separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical and population context as taxonomic/evaluative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributional and population details are important: H. vulgaris is common in Europe and N. America and recorded across tropical Asia; Indian localities (Calcutta, Pusa, Bombay, etc.) and Ceylon records are provided; forms from different regions may represent phases rather than distinct species (e.g., H. orientalis considered a tropical phase of H. vulgaris).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use locality and population data alongside morphological and reproductive characters when assessing species identity or describing new taxa; consider geographic phases and consult type specimens and literature (noting that some older types no longer exist) for authoritative comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of literature, types, and historical records in taxonomic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxonomic decisions and species recognition are informed by historical descriptions, plates, and type specimens (citations and synonyms are listed for H. vulgaris and others); the author notes loss of older types and location of H. orientalis type in the Indian Museum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check specimens with original descriptions, plates, and museum types where possible; compile bibliographic references and synonymies when preparing taxonomic accounts or identifications to avoid misapplication of names.
